name: Cheek fat pad (Bichat) removal

lead: Cheek fat pad (Bichat) removal, also called buccal fat removal or bichectomy, takes out part of the buccal fat pad, a mass of fat deep in the cheek, usually through an incision inside the mouth. The slimmer lower cheek is visible after healing, with hollower cheeks and a clearer cheekbone-to-jaw transition that users link to the ogee curve.

The pad sits between the buccinator muscle and the more superficial masseter and zygomaticus muscles, and it contributes to cheek fullness. Removing some of its volume reduces fullness in the lower cheek, which proponents say reveals cheekbone and jaw structure. The pad is well documented as a surgical flap in mouth and sinus surgery; published outcome data for purely cosmetic removal are limited.

paras: It is a short procedure through the inside of the mouth, usually under local anaesthetic or sedation, with swelling that settles over weeks. It is popular in looksmaxxing communities as a route to hollow cheeks, often considered alongside leanness.

Wikipedia reports a significant risk of injury to the buccal branch of the facial nerve and the parotid duct. Self-performed removal has been described on forums, and other members in those threads warn against it.

angle.text: Buccal fat removal is popular in looksmaxxing communities as a route to hollow cheeks and a more visible cheekbone-to-jaw transition, often tied to the ogee curve. Taking out part of the cheek fat pad slims the lower cheek once healed. Published outcome data for cosmetic removal are limited.

lead: Cheek fat pad (Bichat) removal, also called buccal fat removal, buccal fat extraction or bichectomy, is a cosmetic surgery in which part or all of the buccal fat pad, an encapsulated mass of fat deep in each cheek, is taken out, usually through a small incision inside the mouth. The aim is a slimmer lower face: less roundness below the cheekbone, a more visible hollow under it and a sharper transition into the jaw [1][2]. In looksmaxxing communities it is discussed alongside leanmaxxing, facial bone structure and the ogee curve as a way to reveal cheekbone and jaw definition that fat can hide [3].

The buccal fat pad lies between the buccinator muscle and the more superficial masseter and zygomaticus muscles, and it is the part of facial fat associated with cheek hollowing and the nasolabial fold [1]. Proponents describe it as fat that stays put even when body fat is low, which is why some lean people still have full cheeks [3]. Surgeons have long used the pad as a pedicled flap to close openings between the mouth and maxillary sinus [4][5][6], and researchers have studied stem cells isolated from it [7][8].

The procedure moved from a niche surgical technique to a widely discussed cosmetic trend around 2021 to 2022, when celebrity speculation, a New York Times report and social media discussion drew attention to it; the American Society of Plastic Surgeons began recording it in 2022 [2][9]. A single-arm clinical trial of 21 patients reported reduced facial measurements and higher facial-satisfaction scores at three months, with the authors calling the benefit in patients over 25 questionable [2]. Reported risks include injury to the buccal branch of the facial nerve and to the parotid duct, and because the fat does not regenerate the change is permanent [1][9].

Cosmetic surgical procedure, usually intraoral under local anesthesia [9]

Permanent; the fat pad does not regenerate [9]

paras: Buccal fat removal targets the buccal fat pad, a deep fat compartment on each side of the face, rather than the fat directly under the skin. Wikipedia places it between the buccinator and the more superficial muscles including the masseter and zygomaticus, distinct from the malar fat pad and the jowl fat pads, and notes it is implicated in hollow cheeks and the nasolabial fold but not in jowl formation [1].

Wikipedia's article on the procedure describes it as typically done by plastic surgeons under local anesthesia in about 30 minutes, through a small cut inside the mouth near the second upper molar. The fat is eased out, sealed at its base and removed, and the cut is closed with dissolving stitches. It is often done alone, and sometimes together with a facelift, chin implant, neck lift, chin liposuction or fat grafting [9]. Swelling usually lasts a few days and is often not visible from outside, with the final shape settling over up to three months [9]. Insurance rarely covers it because it is cosmetic [9].

The pad is commonly described as having anterior, intermediate and posterior lobes with sublevator, melolabial, buccal and pterygoid extensions, though there is no single agreed nomenclature [1]. The anterior lobe surrounds the parotid duct, and the intermediate lobe is reported to lose notable volume between childhood and adulthood [1]. Proposed functions include aiding suckling in infants, letting the chewing muscles glide and cushioning facial muscles [1].

An oral and maxillofacial surgery review describes the pad's history as a flap, its anatomy, indications and contraindications, the technique used to harvest it, and possible complications [6]. Because the pad is easily reached from the mouth, it became established in oroantral fistula closure and maxillary and palatal surgery [4][5].

Wikipedia's article on the procedure says Lorenz Heister described the pad in 1732 and treated it as glandular tissue, and that Xavier Bichat correctly identified it as fat in 1802; the pad now carries his name [9]. Bichat (1771-1802) was a French anatomist and pathologist known as a founder of histology, who died aged 30.

Reconstructive surgeons used the pad as a flap long before cosmetic reduction was popular, and the aesthetic literature discusses it in facial recontouring and facelift planning [1][10]. A cosmetic intraoral removal technique was the subject of a registered trial, NCT03974373, which started in April 2016 with 40 participants and is listed as completed [11].

subs.h: Rise as a social media trend
paras: Chrissy Teigen disclosed in 2021 that she had the procedure, and public speculation linked it to other celebrities, including Bella Hadid, Lea Michele and Khloe Kardashian [9]. In December 2022 the New York Times reported growing popularity driven by Twitter and TikTok [9]. The American Society of Plastic Surgeons began tracking it in 2022 and recorded 4,543 procedures that year, the least common facial procedure in its statistics [9]. The online nickname 'Handsome Squidward surgery' refers to an exaggerated face from a SpongeBob SquarePants episode [9].

A 2023 single-arm, CONSORT-guided clinical trial in Clinical Oral Investigations enrolled 21 patients who had partial removal of the Bichat fat pad and followed them for up to three months. It measured pain, rescue medication use, mouth opening, linear facial measurements, quality of life (OHIP-14) and satisfaction with facial appearance (FACE-Q) [2]. Pain peaked about two hours after surgery and returned to baseline roughly ten hours later, and rescue medication use fell significantly by 72 hours [2]. Mouth opening decreased at 24 hours and returned to baseline by one month [2].

All linear facial measurements decreased significantly at one or three months, and both quality-of-life and FACE-Q satisfaction scores improved at one month [2]. Patients older than 25 showed a significant decline in FACE-Q satisfaction by the end of follow-up, and the authors described efficacy in that group as questionable [2].

A separate trial registered as NCT03974373, evaluating postoperative outcomes of an intraoral removal technique in 40 participants, is listed as completed, and no results from it have been published [11]. Most other published work concerns the pad as a surgical flap for oroantral communication [4][5], a systematic review of which found the Bichat flap effective for larger defects [12], and laboratory work on stem cells from the pad [7][8]; these studies do not assess cosmetic removal. A 2023 imaging review describes how facial cosmetic procedures, including fat-related changes, appear on scans [13].

Wikipedia states the removal is permanent because the pads do not regenerate, and that long-term health effects are poorly researched [9]. Because cheeks lose volume with age, it notes that the procedure may later produce an overly gaunt look; options for restoring volume include fat injection, dermal fat grafts and fillers [9]. A looksmax.org guide makes the same points, noting that results depend on execution and that fat grafting can partly restore volume but 'will never return fully to normal' [3].

The 2023 trial's finding that satisfaction declined in patients older than 25 is consistent with discussion of age-related volume change, though the authors do not tie the result to a specific cause [2]. The aging literature, including a plastic surgery paper on combined malar and cheek treatment during facelift, treats facial volume and contour as a whole rather than the pad alone [10].

Wikipedia states that removal may carry a significant risk of damaging the buccal branch of the facial nerve and the parotid ducts [1]. The procedure article adds that nerve injury can cause partial facial paralysis, regional numbness or loss of taste, and that in some patients the parotid duct runs deep to the pad so damage can cause a salivary fistula or saliva buildup [9]. A 2005 study in the Journal of Craniofacial Surgery examined the pad's relationship to the buccal branches and parotid duct [9]. Reviews of the pad's surgical anatomy discuss its close relationships with these structures [5].
The trial of 21 patients reported a mild, short-lived inflammatory response managed with rescue medication [2]. Long-term outcome data on cosmetic removal remain limited [9].

On looksmax.org, hollow cheeks are described as depending on bone structure, the masseter and facial fat, and buccal fat removal appears in threads on the ogee curve as one of several surgical or non-surgical options. A long guide thread frames it as a possible 'hardmaxx' with a permanent effect, spelling out both a more sculpted midface when done well and a worse outcome when done badly; replies include members calling it risky for the average person while allowing exceptions, such as enlarged fat pads [3].

Another recurring theme is sequencing: members ask whether leanmaxxing alone can produce the desired look for someone with a round face before surgery is considered [14]. Forum posts also include accounts of attempted do-it-yourself removal; these are not documented in the research literature and are not described here, and other members in the same threads warn against them.

Related approaches discussed alongside it include getting lean, buccal fat grafting or filler to restore volume, cheek implants and other midface contouring, masseter training and the ogee curve concept [9].

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, buccal fat removal is discussed as a way to achieve hollow cheeks and the ogee curve, with debate about who benefits, whether leanmaxxing should come first and how risky it is [3][14].

claims.claim: Removing the buccal fat pad creates hollow cheeks and a better ogee curve.
Buccal fat stays full even at low body fat, so leanmaxxing alone cannot fix round cheeks.
The result is permanent and can look gaunt with age.
It is a risky surgery that can leave someone looking worse.
Doing it yourself is a feasible alternative to surgery.

timeline.event: Lorenz Heister describes the buccal fat pad, regarding it as glandular tissue [9].
Xavier Bichat identifies the pad as fat; it later bears his name [9].
Hwang and colleagues publish an anatomical study of the pad's relation to the buccal nerve branches and parotid duct [9].
Trial NCT03974373 of an intraoral removal technique begins with 40 participants [11].
Chrissy Teigen publicly discloses having had the procedure [9].
The New York Times reports on its rise through Twitter and TikTok; the American Society of Plastic Surgeons records 4,543 procedures [9].
A 21-patient single-arm trial reports reduced facial measurements and improved satisfaction at three months [2].
